subject: WARNING: model syntax contains ... formulas involving (an) exogenous variable(s)

messages.author: ad66f0af4bd0fbba
messages.subject: WARNING: model syntax contains ... formulas involving (an) exogenous variable(s)
parts:
I used the function "sem" for my data analyis, and got this warning message:

2: In vnames(FLAT, "ov.x", warn = TRUE) :
  lavaan WARNING: model syntax contains variance/covariance/intercept formulas
  involving (an) exogenous variable(s): [MINT MAP];
  Please use fixed.x=FALSE or leave them alone

I still can get some results, but the path coefficient between these two variables (MINT, MAP) is 0.000. 
Then, I did a little transformation for the variable "MAP". I changed MAP to MAP/10. The warning message still appeared, and the path coef. changes to 0.855, and the path coef. among other variables are also changed. I don't understand why this happens.
My question is that: could I use the results with this warning message? If so, which one, MAP or MAP/10 should I use? Any suggestions?

Thanks.

messages.author: af82fa98896529e2
messages.subject: Re: WARNING: model syntax contains ... formulas involving (an) exogenous variable(s)
parts:
Exogenous variables are the variables that are not predicted by any other variables in the model. For example, in 

'y ~ x1 + x2'

x1 and x2 are exogenous variables. lavaan provides two methods to use maximum likelihood. First, it treats x1 and x2 as exogenous variables like multiple regression. The distributions of x1 and x2 are not assumed. However, the parameters only relating x1 and x2 cannot be estimated, such as variance of x1, covariance between x1 and x2, or mean of x2. This method is good if you do not want to assume normal distribution on x1 and x2 and x1 and x2 do not have missing data. This is the default option of lavaan. Second, it treats x1 and x2 as endogenous variables so x1 and x2 are assumed to be normally distributed. The distribution of x1, x2, and y are estimated simultaneously. You can estimate any parameters relating to x1 and x2 but it assumes normal distribution. You may use this option by specifying fixed.x = FALSE. For example,

sem(myModel, myData, fixed.x = FALSE)
